title: Chapter 144 – The Siege of the Doors
html:
[Lin Garden – Lin Yue]

Yue hears her brother come home before she sees him, and what she hears is a silence.

She is forty-seven years old. She has stood in the Garden yard at dawn, for the better part of her life, listening to a place breathe. It is a gift she did not ask for and cannot put down: the soft hum of the seam beneath the cellar, the thin high note of the bell on the tower, the slow murmur of the earth itself, turning in its sleep. For thirty years she has known where her brother was by the pitch of that sound. When he is near, it tightens. When he is far, it slackens, like a string that has been let go.

This morning the string snaps.

She is hanging wet linen on the line behind the kitchen when it happens. A cold high ringing, like a plate dropped in a distant room. She stands with a sheet in her hands and her head cocked, and knows with perfect clarity that something has gone out of the world. A moment later Lin Zhao runs around the corner of the house with her face the color of ash.

"Mother," she says. "It's Kuang."

* * *

They bring him down from the stair on a door.

It takes six of them: Feng at the head, white-faced and silent; Lan Wen and two of the Unkept at the middle; two of the restored pupils at the feet. Behind them a small boy walks with a staff much taller than himself, holding it very straight, like a banner. They carry Kuang across the yard in the thin gray light, and the Lins come out of their doors one by one and stand along the path, and not one of them speaks.

He looks as if he were sleeping. That is the worst of it. His face is peaceful, a big blunt weathered face with a broken nose and a gray stubble, and his eyes are closed, and the corner of his mouth is lifted a little, as if he has heard a joke.

Yue has known him since she was eight. He taught her to throw a punch, badly, in the yard behind the old house, and when she broke her thumb he carried her to the clinic and sat with her all night. He never talked of it again. He was not a man who talked about things. He simply did them, one after another, like stones laid in a wall.

They set him on the long table in the kitchen. Qinghe is already there, with a basin and a cloth, and she does not look up. She is washing his hands. They are huge hands, scarred across every knuckle, and she works over them as carefully as if she were cleaning a child's.

"He told me he would come back," she says, to no one. "He said he would do what he could."

"Mother," says Yue gently.

"It is not an answer. I said that to him. I said it is not an answer." She wrings out the cloth. "He said it was the only one he had."

Yue takes the cloth from her. She does not trust her voice. She kneels beside her mother, and they wash him together, in the cold gray light, with the whole village standing silent outside the door.

* * *

Jian arrives at noon.

She hears him on the hill road. He does not come the way he has come in the past, striding in from the gate with his cloak whipping; he comes slowly, on foot, with a pack over his shoulder and a stranger at his side. It is Pei An, gray and rumpled and shaken, carrying a canvas bundle. The two of them stop at the edge of the yard and stand looking at the people lining the path.

Jian does not ask. He has read it in their faces. He crosses the yard like a sleepwalker, up the three steps and into the kitchen, and Yue, who followed him in, sees him stop in the doorway with one hand on the frame.

He looks at the table for a long time.

"Who did it?" he says.

"The Third of the Second House," says Feng. His voice is flat. "With thirteen Hollow men and a seam in his chest. He's dead. Kuang killed him." A beat. "With his bare hand."

"He held the fifth landing alone for two hours."

"Yes."

"Nobody was—" Jian stops. "Nobody got through."

"Nobody got through."

Jian nods slowly. He walks to the table and stands beside it. He does not touch the body. His hand is hanging at his side, and Yue sees the fingers curl and uncurl, curl and uncurl, as though they were looking for something to hold.

"He had a laugh," he says, very quietly.

Nobody answers.

"I cannot remember it." He is staring at the dead face. "I paid for it. At the glass city, to raise a cell. I told myself it was a small thing. A sound. I thought, I will hear it again. I did not think it would be the last time he laughed where I could hear." His breath catches. "I cannot remember it, Mother. It is just gone. I know that he had it. I know the shape of the place."

Qinghe puts down her cloth.

She is a small woman, and she crosses the kitchen in four steps. She does not embrace him. She takes his face in both her wet hands and turns it toward her, the way she did when he was a boy, and looks straight into his eyes.

"It was like a cracked bell," she says.

Jian's mouth moves.

"It was like a man falling over a chair. He did it very seldom, and it always came as a surprise, to him as well as to you. First he would look quite shocked. Then it came up out of his chest like water out of a well. He would put his hand over his mouth, as if he were embarrassed, and it would go on anyway." Her thumbs move on his cheekbones. "He laughed like that when you were six and tried to carry a bucket and sat down in it. He laughed like that on the road home from the Orchard. He laughed like that the day you came back from the north, gray and stooped, and he said, You look like a boiled radish."

A sound comes out of Jian. It is not a laugh. It is not quite a sob. It is something between the two.

"Say it again."

"Like a cracked bell," says Qinghe. "Like a man falling over a chair."

"Again."

"I will say it as many times as you like," she says. "I will say it every day. I am not going anywhere."

Yue turns away. She goes out onto the porch and stands in the cold with her hands pressed against her mouth, listening to the bell on the tower hum its one long note. For the first time in thirty years it sounds wrong to her. It sounds empty.

* * *

The audience was a lie. Jian tells them so at supper, in the long hall, to forty people sitting on benches with their cloaks still on.

"There was no one there." He sits at the head of the table with his hands flat on the wood. "A gray room in the Registry house at Lower Weir. A table. A pot of tea. A box on the table with a seam in its lid. It spoke. A man's voice, pleasant, very tired. He called himself the Archivist."

"The Archivist," repeats Head Yan. He has come down from the ridge on a litter, in his green robe, with a blanket on his knees. "I remember a title like that. It was an office of the Second House. A very old one. No one has held it in two hundred years."

"It is held now." Jian's jaw works. "He talked for six hours. He was very persuasive. He said that the Gate was dying, and that the House had always meant to finish it, and that it could be finished cleanly if I would give him the third stone. He said the sleepers would not have been harmed." A pause. "He said that he understood my feelings for my family."

"He knew about us," says Wenyuan.

"He knew everything. Which is why I stayed. I thought, every hour that I am sitting here, he is not doing something else." He closes his eyes. "I was right. I did not guess what."

"Kuang," says Feng, quietly.

"Yes."

No one speaks. Down the table, Lan Wen has his white eyes turned to the lamp, and Pei An stares at his hands. The boy who stood on the stair sits between Lin Zhao and Little Bell with a bun forgotten in his fist.

"He will come again," says Jian. "The Archivist said it, at the end, in the same pleasant voice. The Garden is not the door, he said, but it holds the key. He means the cellar seam. The mouth beneath the Mother Tree's roots. If he takes it, he can open the Gate from the south, and the stair will not matter." He lifts his head. "The new moon is in three nights."

"How many?" says Law Elder Han.

"Pei An?"

Pei An unwraps his canvas bundle on the table. It is a ledger bound in plum-colored cloth, fat with pages, each one ruled and ticked in a neat clerk's hand. "The Third kept it," he says. "I took it from his office before I came. It is the Hollow roll. The names the House did not burn. They are held in the ledger, and the ledger moves them." He swallows. "A hundred and nineteen."

"A hundred and nineteen men."

"Yes. In the lowland barracks at Lower Weir, in the cold. They were cattle drovers and weavers and clerks. They have not eaten in two years." His voice shakes. "I wrote some of those entries."

Jian looks at the ledger. His face does something complicated. Yue, watching, knows that look: the quick flat stillness of a man doing sums.

"Leave it with me," he says. "Not tonight. I have little left in the Reservoir, and less in me. But leave it."

* * *

Within a day of the funeral, the Garden has nearly doubled in size.

Yue does not understand it at first. She comes out onto the porch at sunrise to find the road full of people: carts and mules and families with bundles on their backs, women carrying infants, old men leaning on children, a whole straggling column winding down from the pass. Lin Zhao is at the gate with a ledger, counting, her mouth moving. Behind her stands Wenyuan, with a look on his long face of pure bafflement.

"Who are these people?"

"Lins," says Zhao.

"I have never seen them in my life."

"No, Grandfather. They are from the Orchard villages." She turns the page. "The ones who left when it burned. Their grandparents, mostly. Ruyan's letters got to the east, and the Chain's waking got to the rest. They heard the Seat was standing. They heard there was a place that had room." She looks up with a small tired smile. "That is the sixth cart this morning. I have run out of beds."

Wenyuan opens his mouth and shuts it. Then he walks down the steps, slowly, in his mittens, and goes to meet the first of the new arrivals: a gray-haired woman with a sack of onions and a face like his mother's. Yue watches him take her hands. He says something. The woman begins to cry.

By noon the clan roll stands at seven hundred and ten. By evening it is seven hundred and forty. Qinghe turns the long hall into a bunk-house of straw pallets, and the school into a nursery, and the forge into a kitchen, and does not once raise her voice. Little Bell and the boy with the staff carry bundles from the carts until their arms shake. Nobody asks a single arrival to prove a drop of blood. They simply give them a blanket.

"They are not all Lins," says Yue to her daughter that night, as they stack bowls. "Half of them have only a cousin's cousin who knew somebody."

"Does it matter?"

"No." She considers. "I suppose it is how the Lins have always grown. Somebody sits down by the fire and nobody says go."

Zhao laughs. It is a good laugh, quick and clear, and for a moment Yue hears it ring against the rafters and thinks of someone else. She puts down the bowl.

"Mother?"

"It is nothing." She smooths her sleeve. "I was only thinking that a house full of people is a very loud thing. Kuang would have hated it."

"He'd have eaten the buns."

"He would have eaten all the buns."

They stand together for a moment in the warm kitchen, with the noise of seven hundred people going on around them, and then Zhao takes up the next bowl.

* * *

They prepare for three days.

It is the kind of work Yue has known all her life, practical and grim and strangely cheerful. The Lins dig trenches. They stack carts across the gate. They fill every barrel in the Garden with water, because the Hollow men do not fear spears but they fear fire, and they lay a ring of lamp-oil troughs around the wall. Hu, who is ninety years old and has been drunk twice in thirty years, comes down from the forge with a bundle of long iron spikes and a wooden face like a closed door, and sets them in the gateposts one by one with a hammer, without a word.

"Hu," says Yue, on the second afternoon. "You should rest."

"I will rest when it is over."

"You are ninety."

"I know how old I am, girl." He drives in a spike. "I had a good arm. I had a good friend who made me another one. I would like to be of use." He looks at her sidelong. "It's not often at ninety that you're asked."

She cannot argue with that.

On the third day, she goes to the tower.

It is a plain square wooden thing at the back of the yard, thirty feet high, with a ladder inside and a platform at the top under a little tiled roof. The bell hangs in the middle, bronze and green, no bigger than a man's head. Pebble sits on the rail beside it.

He is not much to look at. A gray stone creature the size of a cat, rounded and patient, with two small black eyes and a seam down his middle where something once opened. He has sat on that rail, one way or another, for sixteen years, ringing the bell in answer to her brother's far-off need. She has always heard the bell as the voice of a friend. Now she looks at it and thinks, quite clearly, a lever.

"Pebble," she says. "I need to ask you something."

"Ask," says the stone.

His voice is small and dry. It startles her, as it always does. He has been talking for twelve years and she has never got used to it.

"The Hollow men. Feng says they are held by threads. One thread to each man, from the box. Can the bell cut a thread?"

Pebble is silent. His black eyes go slowly to the bell, and back.

"The bell is a seam," he says. "A mouth. It rings in the seam, and the seam carries it where the ringer wishes. If the threads are seam-stuff, it can ring on them."

"And cut them?"

"I do not know. I have never rung to cut." He tilts his head. "It would be loud. And it would hurt me."

"How much?"

"I do not know."

She looks at the small stone body. She thinks of Kuang, laid on the kitchen table. She thinks of a boy, with a staff too tall for him.

"I will ring it," she says. "You tell me where."

"The bell is mine."

"It is yours. I am only asking you to let me hold your hand."

The creature looks at her for a long moment, black eyes unblinking. Then, very slowly, he puts out one small round paw and lays it in her palm.

"Very well," says Pebble. "But you must not let go."

* * *

They come on the night of the new moon, in darkness so total that the lanterns on the wall seem to swim in a black sea.

She hears them first. She is on the platform of the bell tower, with Pebble's paw in her left hand and her right resting on the bronze lip, and from here she can hear the whole Garden. The slow patient hum of the cellar seam. The nervous breathing of three hundred Lins along the wall. And under it, rising out of the hillside to the south, a sound that makes the hair rise on her arms: a hundred and nineteen thin silver threads, all vibrating at the same note.

Marching.

She knows what to do. She knows it as one knows how to swim, with the body, without thought. She closes her eyes and listens, and the threads come clear one by one, like strands of a rope when you begin to unravel it. Each has its own pitch. Each hums to a single point in the dark hundred yards behind the column, where a pale box rides on a cart, seam-lidded, dripping light.

"There," she whispers. "Now."

Pebble rings.

The sound is not loud. It is the opposite of loud. It is a single high clear note that goes through the dark like a knife through silk, and she feels it leave the bell and run out along the seam, down the hill and across the field, and touch the threads. For a moment nothing happens. Then, far out in the darkness, a man screams.

Not a hollow man. A clerk, driving the cart. A cry of pure animal terror, as the pale box on the cart begins to shake.

"Again!" says Yue.

Pebble rings.

This time she feels it. It is not in her ears; it is in her bones. A deep resonant shudder, as of a great cord being plucked, and the threads begin to part. One. Five. Twenty. They snap like hairs under a blade, and every time one goes she feels the faint dying whisper of the man at the end of it. A weaver. A drover. A clerk. They fall in the dark field one after another, shuddering, and do not rise.

"Yue—" Pebble's voice is a thread of its own. "Yue. It hurts."

"I know."

"It is louder than I thought."

"I know." She tightens her grip. "Once more. Only once. Please."

He rings.

* * *

The gate holds.

She will remember that afterward, when the nights get long: how the gate held. They come against it in the darkness, the hundred who have not been cut, through the oil troughs, which Wenyuan lights with a flaming brand, and the iron spikes, which Hu has set at the height of a man's belly, and the carts, and the Lins on the wall with their pitchforks and their hoes. They are dull and silent and terrible, and they do not feel the flames. They climb the barricade, and the spikes take them, and still they climb.

She watches from the tower with her heart in her throat. She sees Wenyuan, in his wool mittens, with his apple-wood staff, hold the left of the gate for an hour, a tall bent old man in a white shirt cutting down the Hollow men like barley. She sees Qinghe with her kitchen knife, quick as a cat, spinning on one heel. She sees Jian in the center, in his brown cloak, with his eyes half shut, and the Hollow men who come near him drop like cut strings, one after another, without a blow being struck. He is not killing them. He is reading. She can hear it faintly even from the tower. A low steady murmur, a name, and another name, and another.

Fourteen, she counts. Twenty. Every name he reads, a thread goes slack on its own, and a man sits down in the mud and begins to weep.

She does not see Hu fall.

She hears it. A grunt, no more, a short flat sound like a sack set down. By the time she looks, he is already on the ground in the gateway, with his back against the post and a spear through his chest, and the iron spikes bright and dripping around him. A hollow man stands over him, a young one, with his mouth open. The spear is in his hand.

Then the thread snaps and the young man sits down. He puts his face in his hands.

"Hu!" That is Feng. He is across the gate in two strides, on his knees in the mud. "Hu, you stubborn old—"

"Don't," says Hu.

He is smiling. The wooden face is cracked at last, the way a dry log cracks in a fire. His gray hair is plastered to his forehead, and his one good hand, the right, is closing, with great care, on Feng's wrist.

"I held the gate."

"You did."

"I held it a long while. Longer than the boy." He coughs. "Tell him. I was of use."

"I'll tell him."

"Good." His eyes go past Feng, up, to the starless sky. He seems to find what he is looking for. "Good. It was a good arm."

* * *

The sun comes up on a field full of sitting men.

A hundred and nineteen of them, in the gray light, on the churned mud of the south slope, with the dew on their shoulders and the frost on their lashes. They are not hollow now. They are thin, and bewildered, and ashamed. Some are crying. Some stare at the ground. One of them, a weaver of perhaps forty, sits with his back to the barricade and his palms turned up on his knees, and asks every Lin who passes him, in a voice of puzzled gentleness, whether they have seen his daughter.

Jian stands among them with his hands hanging.

He has read perhaps sixty names off the Third's ledger, in the dark, with the blood coming from his nose, and the rest have fallen to the bell. The Reservoir, Yue knows, has paid for it. She can see it in his shoulders. He looks like a man who has walked through a snowstorm. But when the weaver asks him about his daughter he kneels, gravely, in the mud, and answers.

"I do not know," he says. "But we will find out."

On the cart at the far edge of the field, where Feng dragged it before dawn, the pale box sits quietly, its seam-lid cracked and dark. Yue stands over it with Pebble in her arms. He is very still. There is a thin white line across his gray back that was not there yesterday, running from the nape to the tail, like the crack in a teacup. She has not looked at it too closely.

"You rang well," she says.

"I rang," says Pebble faintly. "I do not wish to do it again."

"No."

"But I would." The black eyes flicker. "For the old one. And for the loud one who laughed."

Her throat closes. She bends her head over him and presses her forehead to the cool hard top of his skull, and for a long time neither of them says anything. Behind them, the box ticks, once, like a cooling kettle.

Then a voice comes out of it. Pleasant, tired, unhurried.

That was well done, says the Archivist. Truly. I had not allowed for the bell.

Yue's hands go cold.

I shall allow for it next time.

The seam-lid crumbles. The box falls apart in the grass like wet paper, and the voice goes with it, thin and gray and dry. But the last of it hangs for a moment in the morning air, and she hears it as clearly as she has ever heard anything, a polite regretful murmur from a very long way away.

The Garden is not the door, Keeper. But I know now what is.
